lessons.title: Players and characters
lessons.summary: The Players service, joining and leaving, characters and Humanoids, and finding the player behind a touch.

sections.heading: Players
sections.body:
Every person in the game is a `Player` instance inside the `Players` service. `Players.PlayerAdded` fires when someone joins and passes their Player; `Players.PlayerRemoving` fires as they leave. `Players:GetPlayers()` returns everyone currently in the game.

A classic trap: a player can join **before** your script connects to `PlayerAdded`, especially in Studio where your character loads fast. So connect the event, then loop over `GetPlayers()` and run the same setup function for anyone already there. It's the same "connect, then catch up" idea you've used with attributes.

example.caption: Setting up every player
example.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local function onJoin(player)
	print("Welcome,", player.Name)
end
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(onJoin)
for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do onJoin(player) end
example.explain: Nobody is missed, whether they joined before or after the script started.

sections.heading: Characters
sections.body:
A Player isn't their body. The body is a separate Model called the **character**, at `player.Character`, and it's replaced every time they respawn. It can be `nil` before the first spawn or between deaths. `player.CharacterAdded` fires with each new character, so per-life setup belongs there.

Inside a character, the `Humanoid` controls health, walking and jumping, with properties like `Health`, `MaxHealth` and `WalkSpeed` (16 by default), and a `Died` event. The `HumanoidRootPart` is the invisible part at the centre; its position is where the character is.

Because the character changes, never store a character in a variable for the whole session. Look it up when you need it, check it isn't `nil`, and use `FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")` rather than assuming the Humanoid is there, since it can be removed or not loaded yet.

sections.heading: From a part to a player
sections.body:
Events like `Touched` give you a **part**, such as a foot. To find out whether a player touched something, take the part's parent (the character model) and ask `Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(model)`. It returns the Player, or `nil` if the model isn't a player's character, like a falling crate or an NPC.

Always handle that `nil`. Plenty of things that aren't players touch parts, and code that assumes otherwise errors at the worst moments.

sections.heading: Per-player state
sections.body:
You'll often keep data per player in a table keyed by the Player: `coins[player] = 50`. Clean those entries up in `PlayerRemoving`, by setting them to `nil`, or the table slowly fills with players who left.

Attributes on the Player instance are another option for simple values, and they replicate to that player's client automatically, which makes them easy to show in the UI.

key_points: Connect `PlayerAdded`, then run the same setup for players already in `GetPlayers()`.
The character is a separate model that's replaced on every respawn, and can be `nil`.
`GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)` finds the player behind a touch, or `nil`.
mistakes: Only connecting `PlayerAdded` and missing players who joined first.
Setting up a character once instead of on every `CharacterAdded`.
Assuming every touch comes from a player.
lessons.try_it: Write a Script that prints a welcome for every player, sets their WalkSpeed to 24 each time their character spawns, and prints a message when their Humanoid dies.

quiz.question: Why loop over `GetPlayers()` after connecting `PlayerAdded`?
choices: Players who joined before the connection wouldn't be set up otherwise
It makes the event fire twice
quiz.explain: The event only fires for future joins, so existing players need catching up.

quiz.question: What does `Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(model)` return for an NPC?
quiz.explain: It only returns a Player when the model is a player's character.

quiz.question: When does `player.CharacterAdded` fire?
choices: Only when the player first joins
Every time the player gets a new character, including respawns
quiz.explain: Each respawn creates a new character, and the event fires each time.

lessons.title: Client and server
lessons.summary: Where code runs, what replicates, and why the server must own everything that matters.

sections.heading: Two kinds of computer
sections.body:
A Roblox game runs on one **server** and on every player's device, each called a **client**. The server holds the real game. Each client has a copy of the parts of the game it can see, which Roblox keeps in sync by **replicating** changes.

Replication mostly goes one way: changes made on the server copy to clients. Changes a client makes, like moving a part or changing a value, stay on that client and are invisible to everyone else. That rule, called FilteringEnabled, is what stops one player's device from rewriting the game for everyone.

sections.heading: Where things live
sections.body:
`ServerScriptService` and `ServerStorage` exist only on the server; clients never receive them. `ReplicatedStorage` replicates to everyone, so it's the place for things both sides need: shared ModuleScripts, RemoteEvents, templates. `Workspace` replicates too. `StarterPlayerScripts`, `StarterCharacterScripts` and `StarterGui` hold things that get copied to each player.

`LocalScript`s run on clients, and `Players.LocalPlayer` is that client's own player, which only exists on the client. `Script`s run on the server, where there's no single "local" player.

When something works in Studio but not for real players, a client and server mix-up is the usual cause. Studio's test tools let you switch between the server's view and a client's view during a playtest, which shows exactly where a change happened.

sections.heading: Never trust the client
sections.body:
A player controls their own device completely. Exploiters can run any code they like on their client, change anything they can see, and send any message to the server. So the golden rule of Roblox security: **the client can ask, but the server decides**.

Money, inventory, health, damage, who won: all of it lives and changes on the server. The client shows things and sends requests. If your game would break when a client lies, the server isn't checking enough.

sections.heading: The client's job
sections.body:
Clients are great at what only they can do: reading the keyboard, mouse and touch screen, moving the camera, playing local sounds, and drawing interfaces. Effects that only one player should see, like the illusions in your pizza game, belong on the client too.

A good split is: the server owns the truth and makes decisions; the client presents that truth nicely and reports what the player is trying to do. Attributes set by the server are a simple bridge, since the client can read them and react.

key_points: The server holds the real game. Changes replicate from server to clients, not back.
ServerScriptService and ServerStorage never reach clients. ReplicatedStorage reaches everyone.
The client can ask, but the server decides anything that matters.
mistakes: Changing money or health in a LocalScript and wondering why nobody else sees it.
Putting secret server logic in ReplicatedStorage, where clients can read it.
Trusting values a client sends without checking them.
lessons.try_it: Make a part, then change its colour from a LocalScript and from a Script, and use Studio's Server and Client views during a playtest to see where each change appears.

quiz.question: A LocalScript makes a part invisible. Who sees the change?
quiz.explain: Client changes don't replicate, so only that player's copy changes.

quiz.question: Where should a ModuleScript go if both server and client scripts require it?
quiz.explain: ReplicatedStorage is visible to both sides.

quiz.question: Why must the server decide how many coins a player has?
choices: Players can change anything on their own device
Coins can't be displayed on clients
quiz.explain: Anything decided on the client can be faked by an exploiter.

lessons.title: RemoteEvents and RemoteFunctions
lessons.summary: Sending messages between client and server, and checking everything that arrives.

sections.heading: RemoteEvents
sections.body:
A **RemoteEvent**, kept in ReplicatedStorage, carries messages across the client and server boundary. A client calls `remote:FireServer(...)`, and the server's `remote.OnServerEvent` handler receives the **player who fired it** as its first argument, followed by whatever was sent. That first argument is added by Roblox and can't be faked.

The other way, the server calls `remote:FireClient(player, ...)` for one player or `remote:FireAllClients(...)` for everyone, and clients listen with `remote.OnClientEvent`. RemoteEvents are one-way: the sender doesn't wait for or receive an answer.

example.caption: Server side of a request
example.code:
local ring = game.ReplicatedStorage.RingDoorbell
ring.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, houseName)
	if typeof(houseName) ~= "string" then return end
	print(player.Name, "rang", houseName)
end)
example.explain: The player comes from Roblox. houseName comes from the client, so it's checked first.

sections.heading: RemoteFunctions
sections.body:
A **RemoteFunction** is a request that gets an answer. The client calls `remote:InvokeServer(...)`, which yields until the server replies. The server sets `remote.OnServerInvoke` to a function that receives the player first, then the arguments, and whatever it returns goes back to the client.

Use them for questions like "can I buy this, and how many coins do I have now?". Avoid the reverse, `InvokeClient`: a client that never answers, or errors, can leave the server waiting or failing, so servers should tell clients things with RemoteEvents instead.

sections.heading: Check everything
sections.body:
Everything after the player argument comes from a device you don't control. Check the **type** with `typeof` (an exploiter can send a table where you expect a string), the **range** (no buying minus five pizzas), and **permission** (is this player allowed to do this right now?). Then act, and if the request is bad, return or reply with a failure, never error.

Also consider **rate**: a client can fire a remote hundreds of times per second. Things with a cost, like purchases or attacks, need a cooldown on the server, often a per-player timestamp from `os.clock()`.

sections.heading: Designing remotes
sections.body:
Send **intentions**, not results. A good message is "I want to buy a slice", not "set my coins to 40". The server owns the maths and the outcome, so there's nothing useful to fake.

Keep remotes few and specific, put them in a folder in ReplicatedStorage, and name them after actions, like `BuyItem` or `RingDoorbell`. And keep the logic out of the connection itself: have the handler call a ModuleScript function, so the same logic can be tested and reused.

key_points: `FireServer` reaches `OnServerEvent`, whose first argument is the real player.
RemoteFunctions return answers: `InvokeServer` yields until `OnServerInvoke` returns.
Check the type, range, permission and rate of everything a client sends.
mistakes: Trusting a price, amount or result sent by the client.
Letting a bad request error on the server instead of returning a failure.
Using `InvokeClient`, which a client can leave hanging.
lessons.try_it: Make a RemoteEvent that a LocalScript fires when you press a key, and have the server print who fired it. Then send a number and a table from the client, and make the server ignore anything that isn't a string.

quiz.question: What is the first argument of an `OnServerEvent` handler?
choices: The first value the client sent
quiz.explain: Roblox adds the real player first, and it can't be faked.

quiz.question: Which message is safest to send from the client?
quiz.explain: An intention lets the server decide the outcome.

quiz.question: What does `InvokeServer` do on the client?
choices: Yields until the server's OnServerInvoke returns, then gives back its result
Runs the server's code on the client
quiz.explain: A RemoteFunction waits for the server's answer.

lessons.title: User interface
lessons.summary: ScreenGuis, frames, labels and buttons, sizing with UDim2, and making buttons do things.

sections.heading: Where UI lives
sections.body:
On-screen interface is built from `ScreenGui`s holding `Frame`s, `TextLabel`s, `TextButton`s, `ImageLabel`s and more. You design them in `StarterGui`, and each player gets a copy in their own `PlayerGui` when they spawn. A ScreenGui's `ResetOnSpawn` property decides whether that copy is replaced on every respawn; turning it off keeps one copy for the whole session.

UI belongs to the client. LocalScripts change it, usually by finding it through `Players.LocalPlayer.PlayerGui` with `WaitForChild`, since it may not have been copied yet when the script starts.

sections.heading: Sizing with UDim2
sections.body:
UI sizes and positions use `UDim2`, which has a **scale** and an **offset** for each axis. Scale is a fraction of the parent's size, so 0.5 means half. Offset is in pixels. `UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0, 40)` is half the parent's width and 40 pixels tall. `UDim2.fromScale` and `UDim2.fromOffset` are shortcuts for one or the other.

Scale adapts to every screen size, from phones to monitors, so prefer it for layout. `AnchorPoint`, a `Vector2`, sets which point of the element its position refers to: 0.5, 0.5 is the centre, which makes centring something as easy as a position of 0.5, 0.5 in scale.

sections.heading: Buttons
sections.body:
Buttons fire `Activated` when clicked, tapped or pressed with a gamepad, so it works on every device. Connect to it in a LocalScript, and do what the button means: often that's asking the server something through a remote.

Layout helpers save a lot of manual positioning. `UIListLayout` stacks children in a row or column, `UIPadding` adds inner space, `UICorner` rounds corners, and `UIStroke` adds an outline. Put them inside a frame and its children arrange themselves.

example.caption: A button in a LocalScript
example.code:
local gui = game.Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
local button = gui:WaitForChild("Shop"):WaitForChild("Open")
button.Activated:Connect(function()
	print("Shop opened")
end)
example.explain: Waits for the copied UI, then reacts to the button on any device.

sections.heading: Animating with tweens
sections.body:
`TweenService` animates properties smoothly. `TweenService:Create(instance, TweenInfo.new(0.3), { BackgroundTransparency = 1 })` makes a tween, and `:Play()` starts it. TweenInfo also takes an easing style, like `Enum.EasingStyle.Quad`, so movement can start or finish gently. The tween's `Completed` event fires when it finishes.

Tweens work on anything with numeric-style properties: UI positions, sizes, transparency and colours, part positions, lighting. A short tween on a popup or a coin counter makes an interface feel far more alive than values snapping instantly.

key_points: UI is designed in StarterGui and copied into each player's PlayerGui.
`UDim2` has scale (fraction of parent) and offset (pixels) on each axis. Prefer scale.
Buttons fire `Activated` on every device. Connect to it in a LocalScript.
mistakes: Changing UI in StarterGui at runtime instead of the player's own PlayerGui copy.
Sizing everything in pixels, so it breaks on small screens.
Using `MouseButton1Click`, which doesn't fire for every input type.
lessons.try_it: Build a ScreenGui with a centred frame holding a label and a button. Make the button change the label's text, then tween the frame's transparency so it fades out.

quiz.question: What does `UDim2.new(0.25, 10, 0, 0)` mean for a width?
choices: A quarter of the parent's width plus 10 pixels
quiz.explain: Scale first, then offset: 25% of the parent plus 10 pixels.

quiz.question: Which event should a button use to work with mouse, touch and gamepad?
quiz.explain: Activated fires for every way of pressing a button.

quiz.question: Where does a player's own copy of a ScreenGui live while they play?
quiz.explain: StarterGui holds the template, and each player gets their own copy in PlayerGui.
